According to BILD, the Alabuga complex in Tatarstan is adding new production areas, warehouses and transport infrastructure across more than 1,000 hectares. Russia is also building layered protection around the site, including two rings of towers that may support metal anti-drone nets, alongside several air-defense positions. The factory produces Geran-series attack drones. CSIS estimated output at more than 5,500 drones per month in March, while Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia planned to produce around 11,000 strike drones of various models in August.  The expansion shows that Moscow is preparing to rely on mass rather than precision alone. Thousands of cheap attack drones can exhaust Ukrainian air defenses, force constant alerts and create openings for more destructive missile strikes against energy infrastructure. items.title: Trump Administration Pushes to Remove Tax Exemption for Private Colleges with DEI Policies
items.summary_raw:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is proposing a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide targeted help to students based on their race, a significant escalation in the White House's campaign to eradicate diversity programs directed at Black, Hispanic and other minority students. The Treasury Department proposed the change Thursday in a new regulation that, if made final, would kick in after May 2027. The rule is broadly aimed at ending any policies or programs that help students because of their race, and it specifically says such benefits in admissions, scholarships and facilities “would be incompatible” with the rule. It’s the latest attempt by the Trump administration to pressure schools and colleges to weed out diversity, equity and inclusion policies that had become common before President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a promise to end them. Trump officials have used Civil Rights-era laws to unwind the policies, saying they discriminate against white and Asian American students.

items.title: Minister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warning
items.summary_raw:
Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges people to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as she tells UK citizens to plan for national emergencies

British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.

Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.

As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies, Angela Eagle told the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of having supplies at home.

items.title: Russia's Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan is expanding massively.   The complex, which produces Shahed-copy Geran-2 drones and decoys, has grown by over 1,000 hectares across mul…
items.summary_raw: Russia's Alabuga drone factory in Tatarstan is expanding massively.   The complex, which produces Shahed-copy Geran-2 drones and decoys, has grown by over 1,000 hectares across multiple construction phases in 2025–2026, with new workshops, warehouses, roads, and a separate 450-hectare site south of the highway.   Production has shifted from Iranian kits to largely localized manufacturing using Chinese components.   The workforce pipeline runs through an adjacent vocational college that has used students including minors on assembly lines, with dormitories being built for tens of thousands of workers from North Korea, Africa, Latin America, and reportedly occupied Ukrainian territories.   Counter-drone lattice towers are going up around key buildings after repeated Ukrainian long-range strikes.   The site is under U.S., EU, and UK sanctions but construction continues at pace.  Source: Bild

items.summary_raw:
Event is likely to be largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into a world already in a climate crisis

The El Niño climate phenomenon is “supersizing before our eyes”, the UN has said. The event is near certain to shatter temperature records, according to the latest forecasts.

The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.

items.title: The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less
items.summary_raw:
The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area

Electric-blue meltwater sprays up under Terry Noah’s snowmobile as he races across sea ice extending out from Canada’s northernmost public community: Grise Fiord in Nunavut, a hamlet of 144 people closer to Murmansk in Russia than the Canadian city of Toronto. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay.

Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice.

items.title: US Oil Giant Chevron Confirms It Will Expand Operations in Venezuela
items.summary_raw:
Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it will expand operations in Venezuela after President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits. Chevron, the only U.S. oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said Wednesday that it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations. The company plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day. “Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement. Venezuela holds the world's largest proven reserves, totaling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to OPEC's 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels.

items.title: Pacific Island Nations Seek To Turn Geopolitics Into Funding To Offset Climate Change Harm
items.summary_raw:
KOROR, Palau (AP) — When stormy seas batter Melekeok state on Palau’s biggest island, the Pacific Ocean floods right into people’s homes. “We keep telling the legislature we need to move inward,” said Bol Sebalt, 43, who was born and raised on the low-lying beachfront. “But because of a shortage of funding we cannot.” The fate of Melekeok, a chiefdom of 300 people, is echoed by stories from many island nations in remote parts of the vast Pacific Ocean. Their leaders, gathered for a summit in Palau this week, are wrestling once more with the question of how tiny countries with little global power can use major polluters’ geopolitical interest in their region to secure a chance of survival. Some hope for funding to help them adapt to changes they can’t reverse. Sebalt, a legislative clerk, is also a trained volunteer for her local disaster readiness team, making her one of 200 people across the western Pacific country now prepared to shepherd their communities through events such as catastrophic typhoons that have struck before.

items.title: The Economist reports that Russia has significantly ramped up its production rate of ballistic missiles, and is now producing approximately 100 units per month, including Iskander-…
items.summary_raw: The Economist reports that Russia has significantly ramped up its production rate of ballistic missiles, and is now producing approximately 100 units per month, including Iskander-Ms and RM-48U modified S-400s.  Last month, Ukrainian intelligence estimated that Russia produced 65 Iskander-M ballistic missiles in July. If the Ukrainian intelligence and Economist figures are both correct, it would indicate Russia is producing around 35 RM-48U modified S-400 ballistic missiles per month.   When taking into account the new Kn-23 ballistic missiles delivered to Russia by North Korea, Russia now has the capacity to launch weekly medium-sized attacks on Kyiv (~15 missiles per attack) without ever decreasing their total missiles in reserve, while still retaining 40 additional newly-produced missiles, as well as all of their Kn-23 ballistic missiles for attacks on different targets.   For reference, in 2022, it was estimated by Ukrainian intelligence that Russia produced just 3 Iskander-Ms per month. They also did not have any RM-48U modified S-400 or Kn-23 ballistic missiles at this time.

items.title: Britain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why?
items.summary_raw:
Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system

Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place?

Arthur Downing, the author of the new book Power and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

items.title: Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?
items.summary_raw:
In today’s newsletter: Communities from Scotland to India are pushing back against datacentres they feel have been forced upon them, warning they threaten energy supplies and the climate

Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI.

Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why.

items.title: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’
items.summary_raw:
But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere

Global heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion.

The report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the landmark Paris agreement of 2015 was now “unavoidable” and, despite some progress in addressing the human-caused climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels, likely in the next few years.

A separate, quarterly International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report on Iran also sent to member states and seen by Reuters showed there had again been no progress in Iran, where its lack of access to verify uranium stocks since US and Israeli attacks in June 2025 remained a "proliferation concern".

items.title: Oil Giant Chevron Is Expected To Announce It Will Expand Operations in Venezuela, US Official Says
items.summary_raw:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Oil giant Chevron is expected to soon announce it will expand operations in Venezuela, a U.S. official said Tuesday. The official, who briefed reporters on the expected announcement, said that the company’s officials and Energy Secretary Chris Wright are expected to visit Venezuela on Wednesday where the new investment will be formally unveiled. The official spoke under condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House for the call. Chevron is the second-largest U.S. oil company and the only one with a major presence in Venezuela. Chevron did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The announcement comes after the White House confirmed on Monday it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) as part of President Donald Trump ’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry.

In her Monday ruling, Brenda Sannes, chief judge of the US district court for the northern district of New York, sided with Republican-led states and oil interests in saying the state cannot enforce its “climate superfund” law, signed by Kathy Hochul, the governor, in December 2024. The policy required big oil companies to pay $75bn over 25 years for projects to help New York pay for climate mitigation and adaptation.

items.title: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann
items.summary_raw:
The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now

For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying.

The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action.

items.title: Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports?
items.summary_raw:
The chicken liver sponge has sailed through a test of its ability to filter pollutants in a harbour in Spain’s Costa Brava

In the polluted waters of Marina Palamós on Spain’s Costa Brava, Manuel Maldonado, a sponge biologist, noticed something unusual last month: red starfish had started settling in the area.

Nearly two years earlier, the Spanish National Research Council scientist and his colleagues had begun transplanting sea sponges into the port to study whether they could survive in its polluted waters.

items.title: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world |  Bill McGuire
items.summary_raw:
In Alaska, the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the Alps, deadly chain reactions are just waiting to be triggered

You may not have felt it, but the earth beneath our feet is getting twitchier, and global heating is to blame. As temperatures surge and climate breakdown accelerates, interactions between climate and geology are becoming ever more apparent – as marked by last week’s horrific events in Nepal and Tibet. At the centre of his desired policies was a “BYO power” requirement – a condition that all new datacentres would be powered by 100% renewable electricity.

But last week these aims collided with the Queensland and Northern Territory governments’ desire to rely on their state-owned gas and coal power stations to power datacentres.

items.summary_raw:
Turkey says roadmap being prepared to expand Mecca defence alliance

Turkey is working on a roadmap for other countries to join a joint defence pact established earlier this month with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Monday.

Fidan was speaking at a press conference after the first meeting of a key committee established under what has been described as the “Mecca Defence Alliance”.

The alliance brings together Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, three predominantly Sunni Muslim countries that are also US partners, amid growing regional security concerns.

The three countries signed the defence agreement on 7 August in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Fidan said work was now under way on a mechanism to allow other countries to join the pact.

items.title: Pentagon signs seven-year deals to boost missile production
items.summary_raw:
Pentagon signs seven-year deals to boost missile production

The US Pentagon said on Monday it had secured seven-year agreements with General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and Lockheed Martin to increase missile production.

The agreements aim to “increase production quantities and accelerate delivery schedules” for critical missile components used in the THAAD and Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor programmes, the Pentagon said.

The move comes as demand for US missile defence systems has increased amid escalating conflicts and growing concerns over missile threats in the Middle East and beyond.

items.title: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks
items.summary_raw:
Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas

Turkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.

Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.

items.title: The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all | Nesrine Malik
items.summary_raw:
Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.

The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. items.title: Greece Announces Land Use Reforms Featuring Planning Frameworks, One Unified Strategy for Sustainable Development
items.summary_raw: ATHENS – The completion of a spatial planning land use reform covering three critical sectors of the Greek economy has been announced, titled ‘Special Spatial Planning Frameworks for Industry and the Supply Chain, Renewable Energy Sources and Tourism’. The three frameworks seek to establish a unified and coherent approach to land-use planning, with clear rules for investment and stronger safeguards for the environment and local communities. In a statement to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency (ANA-MPA), Minister of Environment and Energy Stavros Papastavrou said: “with the three Special Spatial Planning Frameworks for Industry and the Supply Chain, Renewable Energy Sources and Tourism, we are completing a major reform that Greece has needed for years. We are organizing land use and leaving behind the fragmentation and inertia of decades. We are establishing clear rules where there was uncertainty, creating legal certainty for investment and strengthening protection for the environment and local communities.”d inertia of decades. items.title: Chinese Espionage at British Base in Akrotiri Feared on Cyprus
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – British military circles have expressed concerns that facilities at a luxury hotel in eastern Limassol could be used to spy on the British base at Akrotiri according to ANA-MPA. At the center of an exclusive report by The Telegraph is the ultra-luxury casino resort City of Dreams Mediterranean. According to the report, the hotel’s facilities, particularly its upper floors, could be used as an observation point overlooking the British base, according to intelligence and military sources cited by The Telegraph. A representative of City of Dreams Mediterranean categorically rejected the claims, stressing that the property operates exclusively as a tourism and business resort. The report points to the geographical location and height of the 16-story hotel, which have reportedly raised concerns among security officials and RAF personnel. With certain observation equipment, it would potentially be possible to monitor aircraft takeoffs and landings, as well as the movements of officials and military personnel.

items.title: Dead and Missing After Ship Carrying 267 Passengers and Crew Capsizes Off Kyrenia
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – A passenger vessel carrying 259 people and eight crew members capsized off the coast of Kyrenia around midday Sunday, August 30  as a rescue operation involving the Turkish-occupied north’s so called coast guard and civil defense teams was underway. According to the illegal Turkish Cypriot Bayrak broadcaster, the passenger catamaran was traveling to the port of Tasucu in Mersin, southern Turkey. The high-speed passenger vessel, operated by Filo Denizcilik, departed from Kyrenia’s tourist harbor and, while several kilometers offshore, began taking on water at the bow. According to available information, the captain attempted to return to port but was unable to do so. The vessel quickly began listing and eventually capsized. The so-called prime minister of the Turkish-occupied north, Unal Ustel, announced that 237 of the 267 people aboard had been rescued, seven were recovered dead and 23 remained missing.

items.title: Araghchi calls for accountability over US use of Japan's airbase to attack Iran
items.summary_raw:
Araghchi calls for accountability over US use of Japan's airbase to attack Iran

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called on the Japanese public to hold their government accountable over reports that US military assets stationed in Japan were used in operations against Iran.

Speaking to Kyodo News, Araghchi referred to reports that US Air Force F-16 fighter jets deployed from Misawa Air Base to the Middle East took part in operations against Iran.

“The peace-loving people of Japan should ask their government to be held accountable for the crimes committed by the United States,” Araghchi said, arguing that Tokyo bears responsibility for how military facilities and capabilities based in Japan are used.

items.title: Israel to sign $3.6bn defence deal with Greece, its largest ever
items.summary_raw:
Israel to sign $3.6bn defence deal with Greece, its largest ever

Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion defence deal with Israel on Monday in Tel Aviv, which will provide Athens with an air defence system.

The project, known in Greece as “Achilles Shield”, will become the largest defence export deal in Israel's history, according to Jerusalem Post.

Most of the funds will go to Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which will supply Greece with David's Sling systems designed to intercept heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles and drones, the report said.

Israel Aerospace Industries will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.

items.summary_raw:

He identified private investment, PPC’s new investment programme, renewable energy sources, infrastructure and the use of funding from the Just Development Transition Programme as key drivers. The Greek premier also referred to investment in healthcare, district heating, tourism and livestock farming, as well as the need to create a new productive model capable of keeping people in the region.

items.title: The U.S. has transferred large quantities of missiles and air-defense systems to the Middle East for the Iran war, leaving some stockpiles in Europe and Asia at critically low leve…
items.summary_raw: The U.S. has transferred large quantities of missiles and air-defense systems to the Middle East for the Iran war, leaving some stockpiles in Europe and Asia at critically low levels, according to U.S. officials.  Patriot, ATACMS and other precision weapons have been heavily depleted, while THAAD interceptors and counterdrone systems have also been shifted to the region. Replenishing inventories could take years. items.title: Far-Right British Provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos Arrested by US Immigration Enforcement
items.summary_raw:
U.S. Immigration officials arrested controversial British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos on Thursday in New Orleans, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Immigration officials announced on Friday that Yiannopoulos was arrested at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport and accused him of overstaying after entering the United States legally in May 2019 through New York City. An immigration judge issued a final order of removal on July 22 after Yiannopoulos failed to show up for his immigration hearing, a DHS spokesperson wrote in an email. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” a spokesperson for DHS wrote in an emailed statement. ICE’s online detainee locator doesn’t say where Yiannopoulos is being held but directs family and legal representatives to the agency’s office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a deportation hub for international flights.
